subject: effective sample size of derived quantities

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: effective sample size of derived quantities
parts:
A simulator uses coefficients from stan to produce a distribution of
derived values, estimates of effects. At the end I have a distribution
of the effect size. Naively the standard error of the resulting mean
comes from dividing by sqrt(N) where N is the number of simulations.

But since the coefficients in the different simulations are not
independent, this is very optimistic.

Should I just use the minimum effective sample size of the coefficients?
That seems very pessimistic.

Currently I use a random sample of the coefficients (i.e., not all of
them and without info on chain/step), which also raises some questions.

First, if I randomly sample M coefficients (sets of coefficients,
really) from a total of N coefficients, and the original sample had
effective size E, what is the effective size for the M I drew?

Second, should I not scramble the coefficients and have the simulator
aware of the chains? Then I could apply the effective sample size
calculation directly to the results.

I'm aware that it's possible to compute some derived quantities within
stan, but the simulations are pretty elaborate for that, and also span
several models estimated separately.

Thanks for any advice.
Ross Boylan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] effective sample size of derived quantities
parts:
The effective sample size calculations don't divide by the number
of simulations, but by a reduced number based on correlations. See
the Stan manual for the exact formula we're using --- there are
different ways to estimate it. It depends on the ordering.

If you subsample (e.g., by thinning), then you compute n_eff based
on the thinned samples, which should still be kept in order so that
the autocorrelation adjustment can be made --- it is not kosher to
just scramble before computing this. The resulting n_eff
is typically lower than the unthinned n_eff but higher in terms of
n_eff / draws (i.e., higher n_eff per iteration).

If you do a non-linear transform of the parameters, the effective
sample sizes will change (the change can be in either direction),
because the autocorrelations change. The change can be in either
direction depending on the transform's effect on linear correlations.

You can generate derived quantities outside of Stan, keeping them
in order, of course, then feed them back into a program like Stan or
Coda to compute n_eff (Coda uses a different estimator than Stan).

I'm not sure how to deal with draws from several models estimated
separately. The above only works for samples drawn from Markov
chains with the appropriate stationary distributions.

- Bob
